title: Captain School Program
description: Officer Formation Level II. Functional area leadership, strategic planning, resources, partnerships, and excellence culture.

weeks.title: The Captain's Mandate: Leading Functional Areas
objectives: Understand the Captain's expanded scope across functional areas
Identify the functional areas typically under a Captain's authority
Design a simple organizational chart for your area of responsibility
weeks.lesson: A Captain in the Order is responsible not for a single program but for a functional area — training, community service, administration, or finance. This is a shift from managing projects to managing systems. The Captain asks not 'How do I run this event?' but 'How do I build and maintain the infrastructure that allows events to run well consistently?' The Captain's mandate includes: setting the standards for all programs in their area; selecting and forming the officers who report to them; monitoring performance across multiple programs simultaneously; and representing their functional area's needs to the commanding officer. The Templar Order's equivalent structure assigned Commanders to geographic regions — responsible not just for what was happening today but for the overall health of the Order's presence in an entire territory. A Captain who is still operating as a Lieutenant — managing one thing at a time, personally involved in every detail — has not made the transition their rank demands.

keyTerms.definition: A cluster of related programs and responsibilities under a single officer's authority
The systems, standards, and trained people that allow programs to function reliably
Responsibility for the health of an entire functional area, not just specific projects within it

examQuestions.question: What is the difference between a Lieutenant's and a Captain's scope of responsibility?
What does 'managing infrastructure' mean versus 'managing projects'?
Draw a simple organizational chart for your functional area. Who reports to you? Who do you report to?

weeks.title: Developing Officers: The Captain's Primary Investment
objectives: Understand why developing other officers is the Captain's most important work
Learn the officer development cycle
Apply the cycle to two officers currently under your authority
weeks.lesson: The Captain's most important work is not any program or event — it is the development of the officers who report to them. A Captain who is the best officer in their area but has not developed their subordinate officers has failed at the essential task. The officer development cycle has four stages: (1) Assign — give the officer a specific responsibility with clear goals and a timeline. (2) Coach — meet regularly to discuss progress, remove obstacles, and provide honest feedback. (3) Assess — evaluate performance against the original goals, not against a vague sense of satisfaction. (4) Stretch — give the officer something harder and more significant than what they have done before. This cycle, repeated consistently, produces officers capable of operating without constant supervision — the only kind of officer worth having. A Captain who skips coaching will get compliance but not growth. One who skips assessment will give feedback that cannot be taken seriously because it has no objective basis.

keyTerms.definition: Assign, Coach, Assess, Stretch — the four-stage process for developing officers under your authority
Regular conversation between an officer and their superior focused on current work, obstacles, and growth
A responsibility given to develop a leader beyond their current demonstrated capacity

examQuestions.question: Name and define the four stages of the officer development cycle.
What is the result of skipping the coaching stage?
Apply the officer development cycle to one officer currently under your authority. Write out each stage.

weeks.title: Strategic Planning for the Order's Future
objectives: Understand the Captain's role in multi-year strategic planning
Learn the components of a simple strategic plan
Develop a three-year plan for one functional area
weeks.lesson: Strategic planning is not a luxury for large organizations — it is the discipline that separates organizations that drift from those that grow with intention. A Captain must be able to think three to five years ahead and ask: Where is this functional area currently? Where should it be in three years? What specific changes need to happen to get there? The components of a simple strategic plan are: (1) Current state assessment — honest description of what is working and what is not. (2) Vision — a clear picture of what success looks like in three years. (3) Strategic priorities — the three to five most important things that must change or grow. (4) Action steps — specific, dated actions assigned to specific people. (5) Metrics — how will we know we are making progress? The Templar Order's multi-decade operations across multiple continents were coordinated by something very like this framework — not formal documents, but clear collective understanding of mission, condition, and required action.

keyTerms.definition: A multi-year document describing current state, vision, priorities, actions, and success metrics
Honest description of an organization's current strengths and weaknesses; the starting point of all planning
Specific, measurable indicators of progress toward a strategic goal

examQuestions.question: What are the five components of a simple strategic plan?
Why is 'current state assessment' the starting point of all planning?
Write a three-year strategic plan for one functional area of the Order.

weeks.title: Resource Management: People, Time, and Money
objectives: Understand the Captain's responsibility for all three forms of resource
Apply allocation principles to a specific planning scenario
Identify the most common resource mismanagement patterns in voluntary organizations
weeks.lesson: Every organizational problem is ultimately a resource problem — too little of something, allocated to the wrong thing, at the wrong time. The Captain manages three resources: people (the most precious), time (the most irreplaceable), and money (the most visible). People management means deploying members where their gifts are most needed, not where they are most comfortable or most visible. Time management means protecting the Order's most valuable hours — assembly time, officer meetings, community service — from being consumed by low-priority activities. Money management means ensuring that every expenditure serves the mission at the level of its cost. The most common resource mismanagement patterns in voluntary organizations are: (1) The right people in the wrong roles; (2) Assembly time consumed by administrative business that could be handled in writing; (3) Money spent on appearance rather than mission. A Captain who addresses these patterns in their functional area will make an outsized contribution to the Order's health.

keyTerms.definition: The assignment of people, time, and money to specific purposes in proportion to their priority
Deploying members where their gifts best serve the Order's mission
The discipline of preventing low-priority activities from consuming the Order's most valuable hours

examQuestions.question: What are the three resources a Captain manages?
Name the three most common resource mismanagement patterns in voluntary organizations.
Identify one resource mismanagement pattern in your functional area and describe how you will address it.

weeks.title: Inter-Officer Relations: Collaboration Across Functional Areas
objectives: Understand the Captain's obligation to collaborate with peer officers
Learn the common causes of inter-officer conflict
Practice the skill of peer-level communication and cooperation
weeks.lesson: A Captain operates in a peer environment. Unlike the Lieutenant who reports to a Captain, or the Commander who oversees all Captains, the Captain must work alongside peers who have equal authority in their own functional areas. This requires a different set of skills than managing up or managing down. Peer collaboration requires: (1) Respect for boundaries — the Captain does not give direction to members in another Captain's area without coordination. (2) Information sharing — proactive communication of anything that affects a peer's area. (3) Disagreement management — conflicts with peers are resolved privately and at the level of the peers, not escalated to the commanding officer unless necessary. (4) Mutual support — when another functional area is under-resourced or struggling, the Captain offers help before being asked. The Templar Order's geographic commands often had to cooperate across boundaries — sharing resources, personnel, and intelligence. The Commanders who cooperated well extended the Order's effectiveness. Those who competed with peers weakened it.

keyTerms.definition: Working effectively with officers of equal rank who have authority in adjacent functional areas
Declining to direct or interfere with members in another officer's area without coordination
Communicating relevant information to peers before they ask for it

examQuestions.question: What four skills are required for effective peer collaboration?
Why should inter-officer conflicts be resolved at the peer level when possible?
Describe a situation where you cooperated effectively — or failed to — with a peer. What did you learn?

weeks.title: Crisis Communication and Reputation Management
objectives: Understand how crises damage organizational reputation if mishandled
Learn the principles of honest, timely crisis communication
Practice preparing a crisis response statement
weeks.lesson: Every organization will face a moment when something goes seriously wrong — a member misconduct, a financial discrepancy, a public embarrassment. The quality of the organization's response to such moments determines whether it emerges with its integrity intact or diminished. The principles of crisis communication are: (1) Respond quickly — silence is interpreted as guilt or incompetence. (2) Tell the truth — partial truths that are later contradicted are more damaging than the original crisis. (3) Own what is yours — the organization acknowledges its failures without overstating them. (4) Describe the correction — what is being done to fix the problem and prevent recurrence. (5) Follow through — the stated correction must actually happen. The worst crisis communication is the response that promises accountability and delivers none. The best is the honest acknowledgment that something went wrong, that the right people are responsible, and that the organization's commitment to its values is unchanged.

keyTerms.definition: The timely, honest communication of what went wrong and what is being done about it
The ongoing care of the organization's credibility through consistent conduct and honest communication
The named, specific assignment of responsibility for what went wrong and commitment to correction

examQuestions.question: State the five principles of crisis communication.
Why is 'partial truth' more damaging than full disclosure in a crisis?
Write a crisis response statement for a hypothetical Order misconduct situation.

weeks.title: Theological Foundations of Leadership Authority
objectives: Study the Scriptural basis for servant authority
Apply the theology of servant leadership to the Captain's role
Reflect on the gap between stated values and actual practice
weeks.lesson: Leadership authority in the Christian tradition is grounded in a startling inversion: the leader serves. Jesus washed his disciples' feet — the work of the lowest servant — and declared 'The greatest among you shall be your servant.' The Apostle Paul described his own authority as 'for building up, not for tearing down.' The medieval Templar tradition encoded this in the Rule: the Master was to be the most observant of the Rule, the most diligent in prayer, the most accessible to the poorest member. Authority in the Order is not a reward for service — it is an increase in the obligation to serve. A Captain who uses their authority primarily to command, to be recognized, or to be served has inverted the biblical model. The most convicting question for any officer is not 'Have I met my obligations?' but 'Have the people under my authority become more capable, more virtuous, and more free because I have led them?'

keyTerms.definition: The biblical model in which authority is the obligation to serve, not the privilege to be served
The Pauline principle that authority exists to develop others, not to advance self
Have the people under my authority become more capable and free because of my leadership?

examQuestions.question: What is the 'startling inversion' in the Christian theology of authority?
How did the Templar Rule embody servant authority at the highest levels of leadership?
Answer the 'convicting question' honestly for one person under your authority. What do you observe?

weeks.title: Building a Culture of Excellence
objectives: Define excellence as a standard, not an event
Identify the conditions that produce excellent cultures
Apply the conditions framework to your functional area
weeks.lesson: Excellence is not produced by occasional exceptional effort — it is produced by consistent systems that make excellent performance the path of least resistance. A culture of excellence in a functional area has four characteristics: (1) Clear standards — everyone knows exactly what excellent looks like in every aspect of the work. (2) Honest feedback — people receive accurate, timely information about how they are performing against those standards. (3) Consistent accountability — the same standards are applied to everyone, every time. (4) Celebration of excellence — when the standard is met or exceeded, it is acknowledged publicly and specifically. Most organizations have the first characteristic and fail on the second, third, or fourth. The Templar chapter meeting was the ancient equivalent of the performance review: it was the mechanism through which standards were communicated, performance evaluated, accountability enforced, and excellence recognized. A Captain who conducts this process regularly in their functional area — even informally — builds a culture that sustains excellence beyond any individual leader.

keyTerms.definition: An organizational environment in which excellent performance is the expected norm, not the rare exception
The application of the same standard to every member every time; the foundation of a fair culture
The public acknowledgment of excellent performance; essential for reinforcing the standard

examQuestions.question: Name the four characteristics of a culture of excellence.
Which of the four characteristics is most commonly absent? Why?
Describe the current culture in your functional area. Which characteristic needs the most development?

weeks.title: Navigating Organizational Politics with Integrity
objectives: Understand the reality of organizational politics in any voluntary association
Learn to navigate politics without becoming cynical or corrupt
Apply the integrity framework to a specific political challenge
weeks.lesson: Organizational politics exist in every human institution, including religious and fraternal orders. Politics is simply the reality that decisions are made by people with relationships, preferences, histories, and interests — not by algorithms. The question is not whether politics will be present but how a Captain will navigate them. The integrity framework for political navigation has four elements: (1) Build relationships before you need them — invest in people without instrumental purpose; trust is built in advance, not in crisis. (2) Be transparent about your interests — when you advocate for a decision that benefits your functional area, say so openly. (3) Never trade the truth for an advantage — the officer who wins by misrepresentation has purchased a short-term gain with long-term credibility. (4) Maintain the same standard for friends and opponents — the officer who holds allies to a different standard than adversaries has compromised the institution's fairness.

keyTerms.definition: The reality that decisions are made by people with relationships, preferences, and interests
The four principles for navigating politics without becoming cynical or corrupt
Trust built through consistent investment in relationships before it is needed

examQuestions.question: What is organizational politics and why is it present in all human institutions?
What does 'never trade the truth for an advantage' mean in practice?
Describe a political challenge you have faced. Apply the integrity framework to it.

weeks.title: The Captain and the Community: Building External Partnerships
objectives: Understand the Captain's role in building relationships outside the Order
Identify potential community partners and the principles of healthy partnership
Draft a proposal for one specific community partnership
weeks.lesson: The Knights Templar built their influence and served their mission by forming strategic relationships with European monarchs, the papacy, merchant guilds, and local communities. These relationships were not mere transactions — they were partnerships of mutual benefit through which the Order could accomplish what it could not accomplish alone. A Captain in the modern Order should be building similar relationships: with local churches, civic organizations, veterans groups, schools, and community service organizations. The principles of healthy external partnership are: (1) Aligned values — the partner shares the Order's commitment to service, integrity, and community. (2) Mutual benefit — the partnership serves both organizations' missions. (3) Clear expectations — both parties understand what each will contribute and what each will receive. (4) Relationship maintenance — partnerships require ongoing investment, not just initial agreement. A Captain who builds one strong external partnership per year will substantially expand the Order's capacity to serve.

keyTerms.definition: A relationship with an organization outside the Order that expands the Order's capacity to serve
The requirement that a partner share the Order's core commitments to service and integrity
The principle that healthy partnerships serve both organizations' missions, not just one

examQuestions.question: Name the four principles of healthy external partnership.
How did the medieval Templars use external partnerships to advance their mission?
Draft a brief proposal for one specific community partnership you believe the Order should pursue.

weeks.title: Preparing for Commander-Level Responsibility
objectives: Understand the scope of the Commander's role
Identify the gaps in your current competency that the Major program will address
Prepare a realistic assessment of your readiness for further advancement
weeks.lesson: The Major and Commander programs represent the final formation track — the level at which an officer shapes the entire character of the Order's presence in a region or nationally. The Captain who aspires to Commander must first reckon honestly with what they do not yet know and what capacities they have not yet developed. The Major program will address: advanced strategic planning, governance and constitutional authority, inter-Order diplomacy, financial oversight at scale, and the theological dimensions of senior leadership. A Captain preparing for advancement should be asking: Where have I led well and where have I fallen short? What do my subordinate officers say about working under my authority — honestly? What functional areas am I confident in and where am I still developing? The officer who arrives at advancement review with accurate self-knowledge is much more ready for further formation than one who arrives with an inflated résumé and blind spots intact.

keyTerms.definition: The highest officer rank in the KTKC; responsible for the entire Order's operations in their jurisdiction
The accurate evaluation of one's leadership strengths and gaps without inflation or false modesty
The constitutional and procedural framework within which an Order's senior officers exercise authority

examQuestions.question: What additional competencies will the Major program address?
Why is honest self-assessment more valuable than an inflated résumé at advancement?
Write an honest assessment of your leadership strengths and the gaps you need to develop.

weeks.title: Captain Review and Major Program Preparation
objectives: Review all twelve weeks of the Captain program
Prepare a comprehensive senior officer portfolio
Set clear, specific goals for the Major program
weeks.lesson: You have completed the Captain program. You have studied functional area leadership, officer development, strategic planning, resource management, inter-officer collaboration, crisis communication, theological foundations, excellence culture, organizational politics, community partnership, and preparation for further advancement. Before your review, prepare a senior officer portfolio containing: (1) A strategic plan for your functional area including current state, three-year vision, and specific actions. (2) A summary of officer development work — two officers you have developed, their current status, and what they are ready for. (3) Documentation of one external partnership you have established or strengthened. (4) A written reflection on the theological dimension of your leadership — how does your faith shape how you exercise authority? (5) Your goals for the Major program. The Major program will require you to think about the Order's constitutional structure, its relationship to other orders, and the theological foundations of organizational governance.

keyTerms.definition: The comprehensive documentation of a Captain's strategic, developmental, and theological leadership
The formal rules and processes by which the Order governs itself and exercises authority
Officer Formation Level III; governance, inter-Order diplomacy, and senior theological formation

examQuestions.question: What five documents should be in the Captain advancement portfolio?
What new topics will the Major program introduce?
Write your Captain advancement statement. Summarize your strategic work, officer development, and growth.
